opening.headline: When exploration tasks contaminate the main context, it evaluates the benefits and costs of a structure that isolates the context to subordinate agents and retrieves only the conclusion.
body: For a single request such as "Find out where the authentication module creates a session," the agent opens dozens of files and repeatedly performs searches. Once all this content is accumulated in the main conversation, the user's original goal gets obscured, and after the search concludes, the entire read content follows in every subsequent turn.

In this lesson, we examine a structure where exploration is delegated to a separate subordinate agent and only a summary is returned. You will read the code defining the subordinate agent, learn how to design parallel exploration and result-return formats, and practice evaluating whether the separation is appropriate.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Context separation can be explained through subordinate agents.
The benefits and costs obtained through separation can be distinguished.
Can judge the appropriateness of the separation structure

screens.title: Search operations pollute the main context.
screens.lead: Please read how the main context is filled while processing a single question. The diagram shows how small a portion of the accumulated blocks is used in the conclusion.

visual.alt: A context bar chart illustrating that only a small piece among the many blocks accumulated through exploration is used in the conclusion.
labels: The portion stated in the conclusion (a few lines)
This is all that is needed
Continues to follow every turn after exploration is complete

paragraphs: The user requests, "Find out where the authentication module creates a session." The agent opens dozens of files and repeatedly searches for the answer, accumulating all read content into the main conversation.

Even after exploration ends and an answer is found, the accumulated information is not erased. The entirety of what was read continues to follow through all subsequent turns, and the user's original goal is temporarily obscured in between. Despite this, only a few lines are included in the conclusion.
If exploration is done elsewhere and only conclusions are brought back, the main context remains small and precise. The structure that enables this is sub-agents.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Is the context used during exploration still strictly necessary after exploration has ended? If not, where should it be stored?

screens.outro: Let us consider how you are handling the search results.

screens.title: Are you embedding the search results directly into the main section?
screens.lead: After first thinking through the question mentally and making a choice, the instructor's thought process is revealed. Answers are not entered or submitted.

items.prompt: Are you appending all search results to the main chat?
items.answer: If no separate device is available, the tool result is automatically appended to the main dialog. It ends up in a state as if everything has been concatenated unintentionally. This becomes the starting point for separating exploration tasks.

items.prompt: How much does the portion used in the final conclusion amount to?
items.answer: In most explorations, what is written in the conclusion consists of only a small portion of the material read. The rest represents the process leading to the conclusion. Once the conclusion is reached, this process is no longer necessary in the main flow.

items.prompt: If there is a separate worker responsible for searching, what form of result do you want to receive?
items.answer: It's straightforward to think about delegating an investigation to a human colleague. You'll likely want to receive only the conclusion, the locations of supporting evidence, and areas where confidence is lacking, not the entire document. The return format of subordinate agents is also designed according to the same standards.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the source code to see how the subordinate agents are actually defined and operate.

screens.title: Read lower agent definition: a structure that returns only a summary
screens.lead: An example of defining and calling subordinate agents for exploration within the Claude Agent SDK. Select the comments next to the code to verify the role each part plays in the separation.

visual.alt: Two context diagrams: the main agent delegates exploration queries, and the subordinate agent returns only a summary after exploring within its own context.
labels: You may use tens of thousands of tokens.

data.code:
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AgentDefinition

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Agent"],
    agents={
        "code-explorer": AgentDefinition(
            description="Used when exploring a codebase to find locations and call paths.",
            prompt="File path answering the question and two core functions,"
                   "Only briefly states the uncertain points.",
            tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"],
            model="sonnet",
        ),
    },
)

async for message in query(
    prompt="Find where the authentication module creates a session using code-explorer.",
    options=options,
):
    print(message)

notes.note: An agent is a tool that invokes subordinate agents. allowed_tools defines approval rules for tools rather than their existence. Removing an agent from the list does not necessarily disable delegation functionality.

The description serves as the basis for the main agent to determine when to use the subordinate agent. If the description is ambiguous, the main agent may fail to invoke the agent when needed or invoke it at the wrong time.

This is the prompt for subordinate agents. Here, we define the return format. By providing only file paths, a few core functions, and points of uncertainty, summaries become concise and useful. Without a defined format, the content is simply expanded in length, reducing the benefits of separation.

Only read-only tools are provided. Since the exploration sub-agent cannot modify files, this prevents accidental changes to code during exploration. If omitted, the sub-agent inherits all writable tools.

It designates a subordinate agent from the main request to delegate responsibilities. The subordinate agent starts a new conversation, and intermediate tool calls along with their results remain within that conversation, with only the final message being returned to the parent.

screens.outro: Let's see what changes when using multiple ones simultaneously instead of just one.

screens.title: Design of parallel search and summary result return
screens.lead: Select each tab to see the difference between serial and parallel searches, and how to determine the return format.

visual.alt: A bar chart comparing the time taken for three serial searches versus three parallel searches.
labels: Parallel: the slowest one of the time slots

tabs.label: Sequential search
tabs.body: If a single agent performs three independent searches sequentially, the total time taken is the sum of the times for the three searches. Since the content read during the first search is accumulated in the context before starting the next search, the context gradually becomes heavier.

tabs.label: Parallel search
tabs.body: Multiple subordinate agents can operate simultaneously, with the slowest independent task completing first. For example, in code review, style checking, security checking, and test scope analysis can each be handled by separate subordinate agents running in parallel. OpenAI documentation recommends using subordinate agents for independent tasks such as document review or investigating different failure causes, while using the main agent for short tasks or steps that depend on each other.

tabs.label: When tuning is required
tabs.body: Agents that modify the same file must coordinate their changes. Dividing independent work in parallel leads to conflicts. Additionally, agents in a managed environment are delegated one level deep and are subject to a limit on the number of concurrent threads; therefore, they must be designed within these constraints.

tabs.label: Return format
tabs.body: Provides each subordinate agent with a clear question and the expected outcome. Returns concise responses in a predefined format—such as a conclusion, a well-supported location, or points of uncertainty. Ideally, even if subordinate agents consume tens of thousands of tokens during exploration, they should return only a summary of approximately 1,000 to 2,000 tokens.

screens.outro: Now we will summarize in a table showing the benefits and costs that separation is not always advantageous.

screens.title: The benefits and costs of separation, and the appropriateness judgment question
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom, comparing the benefits and costs of separation, and use the decision question in the last row to determine whether separation is appropriate.

data.caption: Benefits, costs, and decision questions of context separation
rows: Search results are not accumulated in the main queue but instead complete independently within the slowest single time unit.
Each subordinate agent is given specialized instructions and is allowed to access only the necessary tools, treated as read-only.
Additional calls and tokens, tuning complexity
The main component may shrink, but the total number of tokens can increase, and design for delegation and composition is necessary.
Since the main view does not display the original, you must open it directly again if details are needed.
Tasks that share the same context or have significant dependencies
If all agents need to have the same information, then separation effectiveness is lost.
Is the search content necessary again from the main section, can it be independently divided, or is a summary sufficient?
If all three questions are yes, then the benefits of separation exceed the costs.
data.notes: If you answer "no" to any of the three judgment questions, you should reconsider the separation. The purpose of this table is to compare benefits and costs side by side.

screens.outro: Let's apply this standard to the codebase exploration scenario.

screens.title: Explanation: Delegating codebase exploration to subordinate agents
screens.lead: The source explains step-by-step the process of delegating the task of exploring the codebase to subordinate agents in order to modify the authentication flow. Please follow along by selecting the right arrow.

visual.alt: A bar chart showing how the length of the main context and the subordinate agent context varies across stages.
labels: Reading and searching dozens of files

steps.title: situation
steps.body: To change the authentication flow, you must first understand where the session is created and which path it is called through. This requires reading and searching through dozens of files. If you do this manually, all the contents remain in the main context, making the subsequent modification work context-heavy.

steps.title: Step 1: Clearly delegate the question
steps.body: The main agent clearly delegates questions to a exploration sub-agent equipped with only read-only tools. For example, it instructs the sub-agent to find the function that creates a session and its call path, reporting only file paths and core functions, while omitting uncertain details. If the question is ambiguous, the sub-agent will unnecessarily expand its exploration.

steps.title: Step 2: Explore within self-context
steps.body: The subordinate agent starts a new conversation, reads and searches dozens of files within its own context. This process could consume tens of thousands of tokens. However, this content remains within the subordinate agent and does not affect the main context.

steps.title: Step 3: Return Summary
steps.body: The final message from the subordinate agent returns a summary containing the file path, a few core functions, and some uncertainties. It is important to include the uncertainties. If uncertain aspects are hidden and only conclusions are provided, the main agent will build its plan based on a flawed premise.

steps.title: Step 4: Main Process Follow-up Actions
steps.body: The main contributor drafts a revision plan based on the summary and opens only the necessary files directly. When additional details not present in the summary are required, the corresponding file is reopened to verify the content. In this case, only the read content is incorporated into the main context, ensuring it remains concise and accurate.

steps.title: Cost verification
steps.body: There are costs associated with separation. Additional calls to subordinate agents and tokens are introduced, and details omitted in the summary are invisible to the main agent. In this case, the exploration content is no longer needed during the modification process, exploration is independent, and the summary is sufficient—thus, we can affirm this for all three questions.

steps.title: Counterexample
steps.body: If the task involves fixing a minor bug in a single file, where the file being read is small and the exploration content is directly rewritten back upon modification, using subordinate agents only increases the number of calls without providing any benefit. When answering the third question—whether the exploration content is again needed by the main process—with a yes, it is appropriate not to separate the process.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: Exploration separates and draws only conclusions, thereby keeping the main context focused on the original goal in a minimal way. The appropriateness of separation is judged not by the structure's elegance, but by three questions. Verify that the exploration content does not need to be rewritten, can be shared, and can be adequately summarized.

screens.outro: We will conclude by summarizing the core point in one sentence.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Exploration separates and brings only conclusions.
screens.lead: We organize the criteria for context isolation.

paragraphs: A child agent is a separate agent launched by the main agent to take on a specific subtask. It starts a new conversation, operates within its own context, retains intermediate tool calls and results internally, and only returns a final summary message to its parent. Thus, even if thousands of tokens are used for exploration, the main context remains small.

The benefits of separation are main context protection, parallelism, and dedicated instructions and tools limitations. The trade-offs include additional calls, tokens, and calibration complexity, as well as loss of details in summaries. It is not suitable for scenarios where all agents must share the same context or have high dependencies. Appropriateness is judged by three questions: does the exploration content need to be reaccessed from the main context, can it be independently partitioned, and is it sufficient to be conveyed via summary alone.

When designing, clearly define the delegation questions, conclude the return format with conclusion, evidence location, and uncertainty points, and allow subordinate agents only the necessary tools. One way to identify the first candidate for separation is to examine the current main context input and determine which parts are only used for conclusions and which are no longer needed.

After introducing separation, you must verify its effectiveness. Compare the main context to ensure it has actually become smaller, check whether the main file is being reopened due to missing details in the summary, and evaluate how the total tokens and time have changed. If the main file is frequently reopened, adjust the summary's return format to include more location information and also retrieve the necessary file paths. If effectiveness is not confirmed, it is also a valid decision to revert the separation.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Sub-agents are not cost-saving devices but context protection devices. Do not forget that the total tokens can actually increase.

glossary.def: A separate agent instance that the main agent spawns to take on dedicated partial tasks.
This involves dividing the intermediate exploration content of subordinate agents so that it does not accumulate in the main context.
The child agent simply returns to its parent, in its final message, a concise conclusion along with the location of the evidence.
It involves multiple subordinate agents conducting independent explorations simultaneously.

misconceptions.myth: Sub-agents share the same context as the main agent.
misconceptions.fact: Each new conversation starts independently, and intermediate records remain within the child agents. Only the final message is returned to the parent.

misconceptions.myth: Splitting reduces the number of tokens.
misconceptions.fact: Even if the main context is small, the total tokens may increase due to tokens used by subordinate agents.

misconceptions.myth: You just need a summary to always be sufficient.
misconceptions.fact: If any details are needed that are not covered in the summary, the main document must be reopened and the relevant sections accessed directly.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Exploration separates and retrieves only conclusions.
Sub-agents operate within their own context and only return summaries.
Parallelism and context protection are beneficial, but at the cost of token expenses and detailed losses.
Judgment is made by separating the inquiry into three questions: reusability, independence, and sufficiency of summarization.

closing.reflection: What among the items entering my main context is used only for conclusions?

checks.q: After a subagent has read dozens of files and finished exploring, what is returned to the parent (main) agent?
options: The last message from the subordinate agent, that is, the summary
Contents of all read files and results from tools entirety
Intermediate tool call records of subordinate agents
Dedicated instructions and tool list for subordinate agents
checks.explain: Sub-agents start a new conversation and retain intermediate tool calls and their results within that conversation, returning only a summary to the parent. Thus, the main context remains small.

wrong.1: Once everything has resumed, the main context becomes corrupted, making the concept of separation meaningless.
wrong.2: Intermediate records remain within subordinate agents and are not passed up to parents.
wrong.3: Guidelines and tools are subordinate agent configurations and are not return values.

checks.q: Let's sequentially outline the flow of delegating codebase exploration to subordinate agents.
items: Delegates a clear question to a subordinate agent that has a primary read-only tool.
A subordinate agent reads and searches files within its own context.
Returns a summary containing only file path, core functions, and uncertainties
Main summary to revise the plan and directly connect only to necessary files
checks.explain: Exploration by separating and concluding allows the main context to remain narrowly focused on the original goal.
